subject: physics
timingNote: Higher Level: 2h 30m, 300 marks (60% of your grade). The Physics in Practice Investigation is the other 40% (200 marks). It is a written report on a brief the SEC sets, and for 2027 it is due to your teacher by Friday 11 December 2026, so check it first, see the Physics in Practice Investigation guide. This is the first year of the new Physics course, so there are no past papers in this format. This guide is built from the four SEC sample papers (two Higher, two Ordinary), published in April 2025, and the NCCA specification. The SEC has not published marking schemes for the sample papers, so every mark value for a part below is an estimate and is labelled as one. Ordinary Level has the same shape (2h 30m, 300 marks, Question 1 plus five others) with more guided questions, and the same investigation is assessed at the level you sit.

examDay.task: Written paper: 2h 30m, 300 marks. The SEC 2027 timetable was not published when this guide was written (the exams.ie 2027 timetable page says it has not been released), so the 9:30 start below is a placeholder; the 2026 old-course Physics paper was on 17 June 2026 at 9:30 (third-party timetable, not the SEC). You write in a completion booklet with answer boxes under each part. The booklet is scanned and marked on screen, so anything outside the answer areas may not be seen. Pencil is allowed for sketches, graphs and diagrams only. The superintendent gives you the Formulae and Tables booklet and takes it back. You may not bring your own. Write the make and model of your calculator on the front.
facts: There are seven questions, each worth 50 marks. Question 1 is compulsory and you answer any five of Questions 2 to 7. Six questions at 50 marks make 300. Choose your five in the first five minutes.

Physics is on the new NCCA specification, examined for the first time in June 2027. The old course (3 hours, 400 marks) is gone. Expect questions on models, verifying and evaluating from data, error and units, and on sustainability, health and technology.

It is your source of constants, symbols, particle data and tables. Some questions name pages (Sample 2 cites pages 46, 47 and 83, and 74 and 75) and some do not. Constants are not printed on the front of the paper. Know where each section is before the exam.

Same: 2h 30m, 300 marks, Question 1 plus five others. More ticks, circles, fill-ins, completing diagrams and formula-selection parts. Higher asks you to explain, derive, evaluate and use unfamiliar data with less support.

timeline.label: Choose
timeline.detail: Read all seven questions. Pick your five from Questions 2 to 7. Pick the ones with a calculation you can start straight away.

timeline.label: Question 1
timeline.detail: Six parts (a) to (f), each from a different strand, so about 4 minutes each. Compulsory, so bank the marks first. Sample 1 and Sample 2 both have six parts. Part marks are not printed, so this split is an estimate.

timeline.label: Question 2
timeline.detail: Start with your strongest. About 29 seconds a mark.

timeline.label: Question 3
timeline.detail: When 24 minutes are up, move on. Come back at the end.

timeline.label: Question 4
timeline.detail: Long context questions (such as Sample 1 Q3 with ten parts) are best done in order, because later parts reuse earlier answers.

timeline.label: Question 5
timeline.detail: Show the formula, the substitution and the unit on every calculation.

timeline.label: Question 6
timeline.detail: Attempt every part. Use the last minutes to go back to blanks and check units.

tips.timing: About 25 minutes, roughly 4 minutes for each of the six parts. Question 1 is one sixth of the paper and everyone has to do it.
tips.structure: Both Higher samples have six parts, (a) to (f), and each part is a run of short items from a different strand: light and mirrors, circuits, forces, gravity, magnetism, nuclear (Sample 1), or strings, energy and power, measurement, particles, heat and electric fields (Sample 2). The SEC prints no marks per part, so judge the depth by the size of the answer box. No marking scheme is published for the sample papers, so mark values here are estimates.
reminders: Show supporting work and units. The front page says you may lose marks without them
Use the Formulae and Tables booklet for constants such as c, g and particle masses. They are not printed on the paper
Write only in the answer boxes. The booklet is scanned and writing outside may not be seen
If a part is a weak topic, finish the others first. Question 1 mixes strands on purpose

questionTypes.name: Tick one box, circle, or rank
questionTypes.where: Question 1 of both Higher samples, and spread through the longer questions. Sample 1 Q1(b)(ii) circle the dimmest bulb, Q1(e)(ii) 'the same / lower / varying / higher', Q5(c)(ii) rank four transitions by wavelength, Q7(a)(iv) rank field strengths. Sample 2 Q1(a)(ii) pick the new frequency, Q1(c)(ii) accuracy, precision or both.
questionTypes.see: 'Draw a tick in one box only to complete the statement.' Then a line labelled Justification. Sample 2 Q1(b)(ii): the kinetic energy of the wind after a turbine is lower, the same, varying or higher. Sample 1 Q7(a)(v): pick the new force from six fractions after one charge doubles and the distance triples.
questionTypes.marked: The papers print no marks. By the wording, the tick is one mark and the justification is the second. Ticking two boxes means no mark for the tick.
questionTypes.play: Decide the answer from the physics, then tick once. If there is a Justification line, write one sentence that names the law or the relationship (for example 'force is proportional to Q1Q2 over d squared, so 2 x 1/9').
traps: Ticking two boxes. The instruction says one box only
Leaving the Justification line blank after a correct tick. The line is there because it carries marks
Choosing 'the same' without saying what is conserved or constant

questionTypes.name: Explain what is meant by (definitions)
questionTypes.where: Question 1 and the start of longer parts. Sample 2 Q1(e)(i) specific heat capacity and specific latent heat, Q5(i) refraction, Q5(vi) critical angle, Q6(i) resistance, Q7(i) and (ii) the laws of conservation of momentum and energy. Sample 1 Q6(a)(i) diffraction, Q7(a)(i) electric field, Q5(a)(i)(a) the photoelectric effect.
questionTypes.see: 'Explain what is meant by the Doppler effect.' 'State the law of conservation of momentum.' 'Explain what is meant by a specific latent heat.' In Ordinary Level the same idea is a fill-in sentence, for example 'Complete the following definition of radioactivity' (OL Sample 1 Q2(a)(i)).
questionTypes.marked: Not published. Expect one mark per key idea. A definition of a quantity usually needs the quantity, the change or condition, and the unit.
questionTypes.play: Write the definition in one sentence, then add the unit if it is a quantity. Specific heat capacity: the energy needed to raise 1 kg by 1 K, J kg-1 K-1. Latent heat: the energy to change state of 1 kg with no change in temperature.
traps: Missing the '1 kg' or 'no temperature change' that makes the definition exact
Defining a word by itself (resistance is when something resists)
Writing a paragraph. Extra wrong detail can cost the mark you had

questionTypes.name: Short calculations with the data booklet
questionTypes.where: Question 1 and inside longer questions. Sample 1 Q1(b)(i) effective resistance of a mixed network, Q1(c)(iii) tension in a lift cable, Q1(d) g and escape velocity 900 km up, Q1(f) binding energy of Cu-63. Sample 2 Q1(c)(i) percentage error, Q1(e)(iii) final temperature of 25 g of ice given 15 kJ.
questionTypes.see: Sample 1 Q1(c)(iii): total mass 800 kg, lift accelerating upwards at 1.5 m s-2, find the tension. Sample 1 Q1(f): given the mass of a Cu-63 nucleus, find the binding energy (you must pull the nucleon masses and c from the booklet). Sample 2 Q1(e)(iii): melt the ice first with the latent heat, then use what is left to heat the water.
questionTypes.marked: Not published. The paper says you may lose marks without supporting work and without correct units. Treat each line of working, the substitution, the answer and the unit as separate marks.
questionTypes.play: Write the formula, substitute with units, give the answer with a unit. For multi-stage ones (ice) do each stage on its own line. Constants such as c, g, h and particle masses are in the booklet, not on the front of the paper.
traps: No unit on the final answer. The front page warns about it
Skipping the working. 'You may lose marks if your solutions do not include relevant supporting work'
Forgetting the second stage (ice melts, then the water warms)
Using 9.8 when the question gives 9.81 (Sample 1 uses both)

questionTypes.name: Draw, sketch or complete a diagram
questionTypes.where: Question 1 of both Higher samples. Sample 1 Q1(a)(i) rays to a mirror, Q1(a)(ii) ray diagram for a convex lens to scale, Q1(c)(ii) force vectors on a roller coaster at top and bottom of a loop, Q1(e)(i) solenoid field. Sample 2 Q1(a)(i) second harmonic on a string, Q1(f)(iii) new electron path when voltage rises.
questionTypes.see: 'By choosing a suitable scale, draw a ray diagram below to determine an approximate image distance.' 'Draw labelled vectors on the diagram to represent the forces acting on the car at the top of the loop.' 'Sketch the magnetic field generated by the current I.'
questionTypes.marked: Not published. Expect marks for the correct shape, the labels, and arrows on field lines or forces.
questionTypes.play: Pencil is allowed for sketches, graphs and diagrams only. Use a ruler for rays, put arrowheads on every ray, field line and force, and label each vector (weight, normal reaction, tension) so the examiner can see it.
traps: Unlabelled force arrows. 'Draw labelled vectors' means the label is marked
Field lines or rays without arrowheads
Drawing outside the answer area. The booklet is scanned and anything outside the boxes may not be seen
Blowing a ray diagram up so it runs off the box. Choose the scale first

questionTypes.name: Models, unit analysis and proportion
questionTypes.where: Question 1 of Higher Sample 2: Q1(a)(ii) how frequency changes when length or mass per unit length doubles, Q1(a)(iii) check v = sqrt(T over mu) by unit analysis, Q1(b)(i) a wind turbine power model and a doubled wind speed. Sample 1 Q1(d)(iii) predict how a rocket's mass affects escape velocity.
questionTypes.see: 'Using unit analysis, evaluate the validity of the student's conclusion.' 'Predict the change in the power output.' 'Predict how the mass of a rocket affects its escape velocity. Justify your answer.' This is the new specification's 'models' language: you test and use a formula, not only recall it.
questionTypes.marked: Not published. Expect a mark for the prediction and a mark for the reason. For unit analysis, a mark for each side's units and one for the conclusion.
questionTypes.play: For proportion questions write the relationship, change only the named variable, and give the factor as a number. For unit analysis, write both sides in base units, cancel, then say valid or not valid.
traps: Predicting without a reason. 'Predict ... justify' is two marks
Changing two variables at once. 'Only the length is doubled'
Saying a formula is 'wrong' because it does not match a memorised one. Check its units instead

tips.timing: Five questions at about 24 minutes each. Each is 50 marks, so about 29 seconds a mark.
tips.structure: In the Higher samples each question has two or three lettered parts with a short story or an experiment, then numbered items. Sample 1: Q2 electricity and a bulb experiment, Q3 heat and solar energy at home, Q4 springs and oscillation, Q5 photoelectric effect and the atom, Q6 waves and transistors, Q7 electric fields and radioactivity. Sample 2: Q2 spectra and the Doppler effect, Q3 lightning and Kepler's laws, Q4 fusion, fission and the standard model, Q5 refraction and optical fibres, Q6 resistors and circuits, Q7 collisions and momentum. Topics differ between samples, so do not predict the 2027 set. No marking scheme is published for the sample papers, so mark values here are estimates.
reminders: Plan your five at the start and do not switch. Time is lost on the swap
For 'verify' and 'evaluate', use numbers from the data, never just words
Read the stimulus. Some answers (percentage error, efficiency, speed of the speaker) use data printed in the question
Cross-cutting themes (sustainability, health, technology) are assessed, so a one-line ethical or practical comment can be a mark

questionTypes.name: Investigation and data question (graph, model, error)
questionTypes.where: One or two per paper. Sample 1 Q2(a) bulb I against V with error bars and a power-law fit, Q4(a) Hooke's law graph, line of best fit, spring constant, area under the graph, Q4(b) oscillating mass and energy graphs. Sample 2 Q3(b) verify Kepler's third law from three moons, then mass of Saturn and percentage error, Q7 collision data, graph of s against t.
questionTypes.see: Sample 1 Q2(a)(ii)(c): 'Evaluate this claim by investigating separate data points and comparing them to the values predicted by the student's mathematical model.' Q4(a)(iv)-(v): deduce a formula for work done from the area under the graph, then verify Ep = 1/2 ks squared. Sample 2 Q3(b)(iv): state an assumption that may account for the error.
questionTypes.marked: Not published. The papers print no marks per part. Expect marks for using the given data, for a numerical comparison, and for a clear conclusion that links back to the claim.
questionTypes.play: Quote numbers from the graph or table in every answer. For 'verify', show that a ratio or product stays constant. For 'evaluate a claim', test at least two data points against the model and state whether it holds, with the size of the difference.
traps: Saying the model 'fits well' with no numbers
Ignoring the error bar when asked for the range of values the student would accept
Drawing a line of best fit through the first and last point instead of a balanced line
Giving a percentage error without saying what it is a percentage of (accepted value)

questionTypes.name: Real-world context question (sustainability, health, technology)
questionTypes.where: Sample 1 Q3 (heat loss, U-value, solar panels, 10 parts), Sample 2 Q2(c) Doppler ultrasound for blood flow, Q3(a) lightning conductor, Q4(a) ITER fusion versus fission with an ethical factor. Ordinary Level Sample 1 Q5 airplane, Q4 atmospheric pressure, Q7 Doppler ultrasound.
questionTypes.see: Sample 1 Q3(iv): door U-value falls from 3.03 to 1.40 W m-2 K-1, doors 1981 mm by 838 mm, inside 18 C, outside -1 C, find the maximum energy saved per hour. Then solar panels: convert kWh to joules, power per area, efficiency, mass of water heated. Q3(ix): suggest two reasons the actual mass of water heated is less. Sample 2 Q4(a)(v): state an ethical factor in choosing fission or fusion.
questionTypes.marked: Not published. Longer calculation chains usually pay per step and carry forward an earlier wrong answer if the method is right (this is how the old-course schemes worked; not confirmed for the new papers).
questionTypes.play: Read the story once, underline the numbers and units, and convert to SI first (kWh to J, mm to m, cm2 to m2). Do each lettered step in order, because later steps reuse earlier answers. Link the physics to the theme in a sentence when asked to suggest, justify or give an ethical factor.
traps: Not converting units (4.3 kWh is not joules; mm2 is not m2)
Using the area of one door when the question says both
Vague reasons such as 'energy is lost'. Name how: heat to the surroundings, panel angle, cloud cover
Forgetting that the 2027 paper tests the cross-cutting themes, so a short ethical or health answer is a real mark

questionTypes.name: Explain or describe with a labelled diagram
questionTypes.where: Sample 1 Q2(a)(iii) why current is not proportional to voltage in a filament (free electrons), Q6(a)(ii) microwaves through two gaps, Q7(a)(vi) charging a metal sphere by induction. Sample 2 Q2(a)(i) how a line spectrum is produced, Q5(ix) why light travels through an optical fibre, Q3(a)(i) how a lightning conductor becomes charged.
questionTypes.see: 'Explain, with reference to the free electrons in the filament, why the current is not directly proportional to the potential difference. Use diagrams and/or words in your answer.' 'Describe, with the aid of a labelled diagram, how an insulated metal sphere can be given a positive charge by induction.'
questionTypes.marked: Not published. Expect marks for each correct step in the sequence and for the labelled diagram. 'Diagrams and/or words' means either route can earn full marks.
questionTypes.play: Number your steps. For induction: bring a negative rod near, earth the sphere, remove the earth first, then remove the rod. For the filament: a hotter wire means more lattice vibration, more collisions, higher resistance, so the graph curves.
traps: Describing the result and not the mechanism
Steps in the wrong order, such as removing the rod before the earth
A diagram with no labels
Using 'charge flows' when it is the free electrons that move

questionTypes.name: Derive, deduce or verify a formula
questionTypes.where: Sample 1 Q4(a)(iv)-(v) deduce W from the graph area and verify Ep = 1/2 ks squared. Sample 2 Q6(ii) derive the equivalent resistance of two resistors in parallel, Q1(a)(iii) check a formula by units. Ordinary Level Sample 1 Q3(vii) state the relationship between sin i and sin r.
questionTypes.see: 'Hence, using Hooke's law, verify that the elastic potential energy of the spring can be modelled by the formula Ep = 1/2 ks squared.' 'Hence, or otherwise, derive the formula for the equivalent resistance of two resistors in parallel.'
questionTypes.marked: Not published. Expect a mark for the starting law, a mark for each algebra step shown, and a mark for the final form. A final answer with no steps scores little.
questionTypes.play: Start from a law you can name (V = IR, Hooke's law F = ks). Write one line per step and finish by writing the target formula exactly. 'Hence' means use the earlier part of the question.
traps: Starting from the answer and working backwards
Skipping the area-of-a-triangle step (1/2 base x height) in the spring question
Not using 'hence'. The previous part is the intended route

questionTypes.name: Modern physics, atoms and particles
questionTypes.where: Sample 1 Q5 photoelectric effect, models of the atom, hydrogen energy levels, Q7(b) beta decay and carbon dating. Sample 2 Q1(d) quarks, Q2(a) line spectra, Q4 fission and fusion, Feynman-type diagrams, standard model. Ordinary Level Sample 1 Q2 radon decay, Q7(b) particle collision, antiparticles; Sample 2 Q7 cathode rays.
questionTypes.see: Sample 1 Q5(a)(v): blue light of frequency 630 THz on a plate of work function 2.14 eV, find the maximum kinetic energy. Q5(c)(ii): rank four energy-level transitions from shortest to longest wavelength. Q7(b)(iii)-(iv): age of a skeleton with 3.125% of its carbon-14 left, then the number of nuclei from the activity 115 Bq. Sample 2 Q4(a)(iii): energy from fusing two hydrogen-2 nuclei in MeV, using pages 46, 47 and 83 of the booklet.
questionTypes.marked: Not published. Expect marks for the right equation, the right substitution (convert eV to J first), and the answer with a unit.
questionTypes.play: Learn the equations that are not in the booklet and know where the rest are. Use the booklet for masses, constants and work functions. For ranking wavelengths: bigger energy gap means shorter wavelength.
traps: Mixing eV and J in the same equation
Forgetting 3.125% is five half-lives (100 to 3.125)
Naming the booklet page wrongly. Some questions give pages 46, 47 and 83, others give none

questionTypes.name: Circuits and electronics
questionTypes.where: Sample 1 Q1(b) series and parallel networks, bulb brightness, Q6(b) transistor as a switch, LDR and thermistor circuits. Sample 2 Q6 two equivalent circuits, six switches, current through bulb Y. Ordinary Level Sample 1 Q6(b) thermistor alarm, Sample 2 Q4 current and voltage for a coil.
questionTypes.see: Sample 1 Q6(b)(ii): complete a circuit using a transistor, fixed resistors and an LDR so an LED turns on when the LDR is in the dark. Q6(b)(iii): 6 V supply, 600 ohm fixed resistor, LED on when the cold thermistor has 2 V across it, use a resistance-temperature graph to estimate the temperature. Ordinary Level Sample 2 Q4(a)(i): complete the circuit using the symbols on pages 74 and 75 of the booklet.
questionTypes.marked: Not published. Expect marks for correct symbols, a working circuit, and a calculation that uses the voltage divider or Ohm's law.
questionTypes.play: Look up circuit symbols in the booklet (pages 72 to 78 are cited). For a voltage divider write V across the part = V supply x R part over R total, then read the graph.
traps: Drawing the LDR where the resistor should be (the LED turns on in the dark only with the divider the right way round)
Ammeter in parallel or voltmeter in series
Not showing the divider formula

questionTypes.name: Ordinary Level: guided items
questionTypes.where: All seven Ordinary Level questions in both samples. OL Sample 1 Q1(a)(ii) quote c to four significant figures from the booklet, Q1(a)(iii) tick the correct estimate, Q5(i) convert 260 km h-1 to m s-1, Q6(c) kettle efficiency from 472 500 J into 1.5 kg of water. OL Sample 2 Q1(a)(i) draw the image in a plane mirror, Q4(a)(i) complete the circuit with symbols.
questionTypes.marks: Same 50 per question; parts are shorter
questionTypes.see: More ticks, circles and fill-in boxes, more 'Calculate' with a formula given or a choice of formulae to identify, more complete-the-diagram. Q4 of OL Sample 1 poses a hypothesis and asks you to predict which line is for the less dense liquid, so Ordinary Level still tests investigation skills.
questionTypes.marked: Not published. The paper is still 300 marks and 2 h 30 min. The difference is in the support given, not the length.
questionTypes.play: Use the booklet pages the question names, copy the formula, substitute, give the unit. Attempt every part. A tick or a number in the box is worth trying even if you are unsure.
traps: Leaving blank an 'identify the formula' part that you can guess
Converting units (km h-1 to m s-1) in your head. Show it
Not using the booklet for symbols or constants when told to
